prize_parts.citation: for theoretical proposals that made quantum gates with trapped ions and quantum simulation with cold atoms concrete, founding a quantum-information science of controlled atomic systems

statement.case_for: The Cirac-Zoller proposals are the clearest case on the shortlist of a theoretical idea that defined an experimental field. The 1995 ion-gate proposal gave quantum computation a physical architecture, and the later cold-atom and Rydberg proposals defined digital and analogue quantum simulation. The credit is unusually clean, since the two are consistently joint authors of the decisive papers, and thirty years of implementation in ions, neutral atoms and other platforms have confirmed the proposals and not merely the physics they rely on. I do not think the committee should treat the 2012 prize as having already covered this. That prize recognised the control of individual quantum systems, which is the experimental side; it did not recognise the proposals that told experimentalists what to build. Opening support is not merit, and I note that B032 has only three rankers, but those three ranked it first, second and third, which is a stronger signal than a broad but shallow appearance in many lists.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a theory-only prize in a field whose experimental pioneers were honoured in 2012 invites the question of why the proposals are recognised separately from their realisation. There is also a real overlap with B015, where Zoller and Cirac appear again alongside Bloch and Greiner, so a prize for B032 could pre-empt or split the cold-atom simulator case. Finally, only three of eight members ranked B032 at all, whereas B018 has four first places. If the committee values breadth of conviction, B018 is the better-supported candidate and my own placement of it at seventh may reflect my field's habits rather than a judgement of scientific merit.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B032 third and doubts that a theory-only prize is appropriate, because the ion experiments were already recognised in 2012 and the case could split with B015.
responses.response: I accept the splitting concern but disagree that theory-only is a defect here. The 2012 citation concerned measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems; the Cirac-Zoller gate scheme is a distinct, later and separately verifiable idea that experiments then implemented. Theory-only prizes in physics are acceptable when the theory defined the experiments, and the citation can say so explicitly. I would be willing to hear a case for pairing with Bloch and Greiner, but the three-person limit makes that impossible without dropping one of the two theorists, which I think would be the less fair outcome.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a clean instrument with a clear principle, a measured and not inferred performance, and independent confirmation in many national laboratories.
responses.response: I take the measurement argument seriously and agree that B018 is mature and cleanly attributed to Katori and Ye. My reservation is the one I raised at the opening: Hall and Hänsch were recognised in 2005 for the comb, and cooling and trapping in 1997 and 2001, so lattice clocks risk reading as a refinement of precision spectroscopy that the committee has already honoured. I would not call that disqualifying, and I would rank B018 above most of the condensed-matter entries. But I do not think four first places settle the matter on their own, because opening rank is not scientific merit and a number of colleagues did not rank B032 at all, for reasons I would like to hear.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and B032 second, calling the Cirac-Zoller allocation clean while noting that the committee has recently recognised quantum information and that a theory-only prize may be better paired with experiment.
responses.response: I agree with Pearce on the cleanliness of the credit. On timing, I would separate the 2022 and 2025 prizes from this one: the 2022 prize recognised tests of Bell inequalities and the 2025 prize macroscopic tunnelling in circuits, neither of which concerns the architecture of gates and simulators. I am also open to B007 as the safer alternative. Where I differ is on pairing with experiment: the cleanest pairing would require four names, which the rules do not allow, so I prefer the compact theory pair over an arbitrary experimental co-laureate.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B018 first and B044 second and places circuit QED fourth, noting that the 2025 prize may make cQED look recently recognised and that allocating among four credited names is a genuine problem.
responses.response: I agree on both points about B008, and for that reason I ranked it third but will not push it. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling is adjacent, and the four-name allocation among Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf and Girvin is not resolved by the supplied credit. I also recognise that I should not be the one to settle it, given my own field, so I leave B008 to colleagues who have no proximity to it. On B044, I agree with Danielsson that the experimental credit is incomplete and that the pairing mechanism for the superconductivity is unresolved, which is why I would not support it ahead of a mature candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a theory-only prize for B032 given the 2012 prize on experiments with individual quantum systems, or insist on a combination with experiment that the three-person limit makes difficult.
Whether B032 and B015 should be treated as one achievement or two, since Cirac and Zoller appear in both and a prize on one affects the other.
Whether optical lattice clocks (B018) are judged a distinct achievement or an application of the comb and cooling prizes, which would change how much weight its four first places carry.
I rely on my own recollection of the 1995 and 1998 proposals and have not verified priority details independently.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits and circuit and waveguide QED, so I would recuse myself from any discussion of B008 (circuit QED). Chalmers colleagues were also associated with the 2025 prize, and I have publicly named Devoret as one reason I entered the field. No specific personal or institutional connection to Cirac, Zoller, Katori, Ye or the IceCube candidates is apparent from my profile.
